title: Learning to Live with a Changing Climate
paras: For many years, discussion of climate change concentrated almost exclusively on mitigation, the effort to reduce the emissions that drive warming. Talk of adaptation, the adjustment of societies to conditions that have already changed or are certain to change, was often regarded with suspicion, as if planning for the consequences amounted to surrendering the fight to prevent them. That attitude has faded. Even under the most ambitious reductions in emissions, some further change is already locked in by the gases in the atmosphere, and communities from river deltas to mountain villages are being forced to respond whether or not they have been given the means to do so.

Adaptation takes many forms, which can be grouped broadly into three kinds. The most visible is hard infrastructure: sea walls, larger drains, raised roads and reservoirs. A second kind works with natural systems, as when coastal mangroves are restored to absorb the energy of waves, wetlands are protected to hold floodwater, or trees are planted to cool crowded districts. The third is institutional and behavioural: early-warning systems, flexible insurance, revised building codes, and changes in what farmers plant and when. Often the least conspicuous of these measures turn out to be the most cost-effective.

No single solution suits every place. A technique that protects a low-lying city may be irrelevant to a dry upland region where the difficulty is too little water, not too much. This is one reason that local knowledge matters. Farmers who have observed shifting rainfall for decades often hold detailed understanding of which crops and planting dates still work, and programmes that begin by consulting them tend to fare better than those imposed from outside. It does not follow that traditional methods are always sufficient; when conditions move beyond anything experienced in living memory, past experience becomes a less reliable guide.

The most serious risk in adaptation planning is maladaptation, meaning an action that reduces vulnerability in the short term but increases it elsewhere or later. Widespread air conditioning cools buildings, but the additional electricity it requires may add to emissions and strain power grids during the very heatwaves it is meant to endure. A sea wall may protect one town while accelerating erosion at its neighbour. Irrigation can rescue a failing harvest while draining the underground reserves on which future harvests depend. Such outcomes are seldom intended; they arise because the effects of a measure are judged over too small an area or too short a period.

Questions of fairness are inseparable from the subject. The people most exposed to climate hazards are frequently those who have contributed least to the problem and who possess the fewest resources to respond. Financing is a further obstacle. The benefits of adaptation consist of harm that does not occur, which is hard to measure and does not generate revenue, so private investors tend to prefer projects that deliver visible returns. As a result, funding for adaptation has consistently lagged behind funding for mitigation, a gap that many governments of vulnerable countries regard as unjust.

There are also limits to what adaptation can achieve. Some losses cannot be offset by engineering or planning: a coral reef that has bleached, a way of life tied to a particular shoreline, or a sacred or ancestral landscape. Managed retreat, in which communities are helped to relocate from places that can no longer be protected, is therefore a delicate subject. Planners may regard it as the rational response to rising seas, but residents often feel that it asks them to give up not merely property but identity. Treating relocation as a technical matter risks overlooking why people resist it.

What, then, does good adaptation look like? Increasingly, specialists favour approaches that assume uncertainty rather than ignore it, building flexibility into plans so that they can be adjusted as conditions become clearer. A flood defence designed so that it can be raised later is preferable to one built to a single prediction. Adaptation and mitigation, in this view, are not rivals for the same resources but two halves of a single strategy: the less warming is allowed to occur, the smaller and cheaper the task of adjusting to it will be.

title: The Economy of Attention
paras: Every era has its scarce resource. In agricultural societies it was land; in industrial ones, capital and fuel. Some economists now argue that in a world where information is overabundant the scarcest resource is human attention. A message or a video costs almost nothing to produce and distribute, but each person has only a limited number of waking hours in which to notice it. The idea that attention can be treated as something to be competed for, captured and sold has given rise to the expression attention economy, and to a lively dispute about whether the arrangement serves the people whose attention is at stake.

The business logic is simple. Many of the most widely used digital services cost the user nothing. They are paid for by advertisers, who in turn pay according to how long people stay and how often they return. Success is therefore measured in engagement: minutes spent, items viewed, notifications opened. Designers have responded with features that are now familiar, such as feeds that never end, automatic playback of the next video, and alerts timed to bring people back. Many of these draw on research into variable rewards, the finding that an uncertain payoff holds attention more firmly than a predictable one.

Critics see in this a systematic exploitation of psychological weakness. They argue that products engineered to maximise time spent are bound to undermine concentration, interfere with sleep and encourage comparison with others. A more structural concern is that content provoking strong emotion tends to hold attention longer than content that informs calmly, so that systems optimised for engagement may amplify outrage and promote division without anyone having intended it. On this reading, the problem lies not in the wickedness of individual companies but in the incentive built into the model.

Others consider the alarm exaggerated. Each new medium, from the printed novel to television, was accused in its day of corroding the minds of its audience, and the predictions were largely mistaken. Users, they point out, gain real benefits from free access to knowledge, communication and entertainment, and most appear to decide for themselves how to spend their time. The strongest version of this defence also notes that the term addiction is sometimes used loosely, and that treating a habit as a disease can shift responsibility away from the person who has it.

The research evidence is more mixed than either side usually admits. Many studies link heavy use with poorer wellbeing, but most are correlational, and the direction of cause is unclear: people who are already lonely or anxious may spend longer online, rather than the other way round. Findings also differ according to the manner of use. Active communication with friends appears to carry different consequences from passive scrolling through strangers' posts. Averages conceal wide variation, and a measure that helps one group may do little for another. Honest reading of the evidence supports caution, not certainty.

Policy proposals reflect these uncertainties. Some would regulate design directly, requiring that automatic playback be switched off by default, or that young users be offered time limits. Others focus on transparency, demanding that platforms explain how their recommendation systems rank content and allow independent researchers to examine them. A third group favours paid, advertisement-free alternatives that would change the incentive itself. Each proposal draws objections. Defaults can be dismissed as paternalistic, transparency is difficult to enforce, and subscription models may leave poorer users with the more intrusive option.

Beneath the argument lies a question about who ought to control attention. In a conventional market, a firm succeeds by offering something the customer wants. In an attention market, the customer is partly the product, and the firm may succeed by encouraging behaviour that the user would, on reflection, prefer to avoid. That distinction, between what people choose in the moment and what they would endorse afterwards, may prove more useful for judging the system than any single statistic about screen time.

title: What Counts as Proof?
paras: Scientists and lawyers both claim to reach conclusions by weighing evidence, and in everyday speech the word proof is used for the result of either process. Yet the two professions use the word very differently, and the difference is not merely a matter of vocabulary. It reflects distinct purposes, distinct tolerances for error, and distinct ideas of when it is acceptable to stop asking questions. Looking at them side by side shows how much the meaning of proof depends on what a decision is for.

In the natural sciences, proof in the strict sense is rare; it belongs mainly to mathematics. Empirical theories are supported by evidence, but they are never conclusively demonstrated, since a new observation may always contradict them. Philosophers of science have therefore stressed that a good theory is one that could, in principle, be shown wrong and has so far survived attempts to do so. Confidence grows when independent methods, applied by different teams, converge on the same conclusion. Statistical thresholds help to decide when a pattern is unlikely to be an accident, but they are conventions, not laws of nature, and sensible scientists treat them accordingly.

A court cannot suspend judgement. A case must be decided, and decided within a reasonable period, so the law has developed explicit standards of proof. In a civil dispute, the claimant generally need only show that their version is more probable than not. In a criminal trial, the prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. These standards are not scientific measures but moral choices. They express a view about which mistake is worse: convicting an innocent person is judged more serious than acquitting a guilty one, and the demand for proof is raised to reflect that judgement.

The two systems also differ in what they permit as evidence. Science welcomes every relevant observation, and an inconvenient result is as valuable as a convenient one. Law, by contrast, excludes certain material for reasons unconnected with its truth. Evidence obtained by unlawful means may be inadmissible, hearsay is usually restricted, and some communications, such as those between a client and a lawyer, are protected. These rules sometimes keep reliable information from the decision-maker, but they serve values that the legal system rates above accuracy in the individual case, such as the integrity of the process and the protection of rights.

Friction arises where the two meet, notably in expert testimony. Courts have attempted to screen scientific evidence by asking whether a technique has been tested, whether its error rate is known and whether it is accepted in the relevant field. Yet some forensic methods were used for decades before such questions were put to them, and when scrutiny came, it showed that certain claims of certainty could not be supported. Scientists are also uneasy when the absence of proof of harm is treated by a court as proof of safety, or when a tentative finding is presented to a jury as settled fact.

Statistics provides a further source of misunderstanding. Suppose a trace found at a crime scene matches a suspect, and the chance of a random person matching is one in a million. It is tempting to conclude that there is only a one-in-a-million chance that the suspect is innocent. That reasoning confuses two different probabilities, an error often called the prosecutor's fallacy. In a city of ten million people, roughly ten innocent residents would be expected to match as well, so the match alone says little unless other evidence points to the accused. Judges and juries are rarely trained to detect such slips, and eloquent experts may not warn them.

Each discipline could learn from the other. Law might borrow from science a greater readiness to admit uncertainty and to revise settled practices when they are shown to be unreliable. Science might borrow from law the habit of stating in advance how much evidence is enough and who must supply it. Proof, in the end, is not a single thing that evidence either possesses or lacks. It is a judgement about sufficiency, made against a background of purposes and values, and it is wise to ask which standard is being applied before accepting that something has been proved.
